newsitem.title: USA: Stock market awaits key economic data.
newsitem.headline: Stock market awaits key economic data.

text.p: A slew of economic news next week will give investors a reading of how the economy finished 1996 and an early glimpse of how 1997 may play out for the stock market.

Meanwhile, some stocks are likely to suffer in what has become a market ritual before quarterly earnings reports as certain companies "pre-announce" results that fall below expectations on Wall Street.

The earnings season will begin in earnest when major banks start reporting on Jan. 13. But next week, investors will be focused on the December employment report, due Friday, and Thursday's report on prices at the wholesale level, also for December.

"The real important number next week is the employment report and the bond and stock markets will be a little edgy heading into this," said Charlie Crane, director of research at Spears, Benzak, Salomon & Farrell.

"The financial stocks will amplify whatever happens in bond market. If we get a weak employment number and bonds trade higher, financial stock are poised to move up. If the bond market remains as sloppy as it has been for the past few weeks, financial stocks will fall," he said.

The Dow Jones industrial average closed the week with an impressive gain Friday, rising 101.60 points to 6,544.09. But the Dow shed 16.82 points in four sessions this week from the record 6,560.91 set on Dec. 27. The week included a drop of 101 points on Tuesday.
A drop in Treasury bond prices, and commensurate rise in yields, put pressure on stocks all week.

The bellwether 30-year Treasury edged up 2/32, or 62.5 cents on a $1,000 bond Friday, to yield 6.73 percent, down from 6.74 percent on Thursday. Still, the yield has jumped nearly two-tenths of a point from 6.54 percent last Friday, and as it nears 7 percent bonds will draw more funds away from stocks.
Bond prices and yields move in the opposite direction.
Crane said he expects the pace of job creation over the next several months to slow significantly "because profits were so uninspiring in 1996."

"If earnings are not growing from one year to the next, companies are not going to build their businesses. If anything, they will be prone to be cut. Given the pace of earnings growth in 1996, it will translate into more anaemic job growth this year," he said.

Regarding warnings about fourth-quarter earnings, Crane said they were unlikely to be as dire as the red flags sent up before the prior quarter, which included warnings from such blue-chip companies as Motorola Inc. and Hewlett-Packard Co.

"The fourth quarter economy was definitely better than the the third quarter, and activity better than anticipated. So I am guessing the pace of disappointments will be diminished relative to the third quarter," he said.
Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross, said the stock market was in "an interim correction" in an ongoing bull market.
"There are a lot of good stocks at bad prices," he said.
"The employment data and PPI only have the potential to add to the volatility" experienced this week, he said.
He said he did not expect any big surprises from the wholesale price and employment reports. But the jobs data could seem stronger than they actually are because of seasonal adjustments, he noted.
